KWFinder, part of Mangools, helps you turn a broad topic into a list of searches worth investigating. Start with a term your customers would actually use, choose the market you serve, and look for phrases that describe a specific problem. A flooring installer, for example, might begin with “wood flooring” and find that a question about refinishing engineered wood deserves a guide of its own.

Compare search volume and keyword difficulty

Estimated volume gives you a sense of demand. Keyword Difficulty helps you compare the strength of the organic results. Read both numbers alongside the results themselves. If Google shows category pages and your draft is a tutorial, the format may be the larger obstacle. Paid competition and cost per click are separate metrics.

Research competitor domains

Use Search by Domain to find terms a relevant competitor appears for. Start with a single page when the competitor sells many unrelated products. Add only phrases you could answer with your own examples, photos, or experience. Check Search Console for related terms that already show an existing page before adding a new one.

Compare a KWFinder discount with direct access

Check the current billing period, lookup limits, and whether access includes the Mangools tools you need. An annual plan's monthly equivalent and the amount charged upfront are different figures. For official features and limits, see Mangools plans. For related research workflows, see SEMScoop.

Start with a decision, not a long keyword list

Before opening a keyword tool, choose one decision you need to make. A small business might be deciding whether to add a service page, improve a product category, or write a guide for customers who are still comparing their options. The best set of keywords looks different for each decision. A service page needs phrases from people who want to hire someone. A guide can answer questions from people who want to understand the problem before they call.

Imagine a flooring company that installs engineered wood and also offers refinishing. Its staff keep hearing customers ask whether their floors can be refinished. That question makes a good starting point because the business can answer it with photographs and examples from actual jobs. The owner can start with “refinish engineered wood,” then look for related questions about sanding, surface damage, and when replacement makes more sense. A phrase that the business can answer well is worth investigating even if its estimate looks modest.

Set your location and language before recording the results. A phrase common in the United States may be less common in the United Kingdom, where people might use a different product name. For a local service, compare a few terms in the area you actually cover. A national estimate can give you context, but it tells you little about whether a customer nearby uses that phrase.

Use long-tail searches to understand the job

Long-tail keyword research works best when you pay attention to the details people include. “Wood flooring” leaves the reader's goal open. “Can engineered wood floors be sanded twice?” tells you that the reader already has a floor and wants to know whether another repair is possible. That extra detail gives you a better idea of which photos, measurements, and answers will make the page useful.

Keep variations together when they ask the same question. A guide can usually answer “can engineered floors be refinished” and “is it possible to refinish engineered hardwood” without separate pages. Give a phrase its own page when the reader expects a different result. Someone searching for a refinishing contractor near them may need a service area, a quote form, and examples of completed work. Those needs are different from a homeowner reading up on the material.

Write a note beside each candidate phrase in your spreadsheet. Use one sentence to explain what the searcher wants and what you can give them. If you cannot describe both, put the phrase aside and look at the search results again. This step makes it easier to hand the research to a writer without asking them to interpret a list of numbers on their own.

Read the search results before trusting a score

Search volume is an estimate. It helps compare the broad level of interest in two phrases, particularly when both are researched for the same location and period. A seasonal query may look quiet in one month and spike in another. Check the trend alongside the average if you are planning a page for a specific event or time of year. Think about whether you need to publish early enough for the page to be discovered before that peak.

Keyword Difficulty is a way to compare the apparent strength of organic competition. Use it to narrow a long list, then inspect the results for the terms that remain. Check whether the ranking pages answer the same question you intend to answer. Look for relevant pages from businesses about your size and for examples of content that offers something your team can match or improve. Record the actual result type, such as a local service, a how-to article, or a category listing.

A low difficulty score can still lead to a poor choice. For example, a phrase about flooring installation jobs might be easy to find, but a business looking for customers would have little reason to write a landing page for it. Likewise, a high score does not tell you that a relevant topic is useless. It may belong in your plan as a supporting question on a page that already serves the audience. Use the score together with relevance and the format people expect.

If you are using KWFinder for paid search as well, keep paid metrics in separate columns. Cost per click can help you estimate what to investigate in a campaign, while an organic difficulty score supports a decision about search content. A keyword can attract many advertisers and still call for a different organic page than the paid landing page you would build for it.

Find better examples with competitor research

Pick two or three pages that serve the same audience. A national home improvement retailer might rank for thousands of flooring searches, but its entire domain is too broad for this task. Start with a guide or product category that answers the question you are researching. If several pages appear for a term, read enough to see what they cover and what they leave open.

Look for gaps your business is qualified to fill. If most pages give a quick yes or no about sanding engineered wood, your team might show how installers check the thickness of the top layer and when an in-person inspection makes sense. Use original pictures or a clear example from your own work where you have permission. A real explanation is more useful than repeating every phrase a competitor ranks for.

Keep the competitor URL and the date in your notes. Search results change and the pages you review may be updated later. When someone asks why the brief calls for a comparison table or a particular question, you can show what you observed and explain how the new material will help readers.

Bring in queries from your own Search Console report

If you already have a related page, filter the Search Console performance report to that URL. Read the queries alongside clicks, impressions, and average position. A query with impressions is evidence that your page appeared for that search. It is a starting point for asking whether the page answers the question well and whether the title describes what people can find on it.

Suppose your refinishing page already appears for several questions about engineered wood but mostly talks about solid hardwood. Check whether you can expand the page with a clear section for engineered floors. If the questions call for a different page with detailed examples, build that guide and link to it from the service page. An impression by itself does not tell you which of those changes will work. Read the page and the results together before choosing.

Compare similar periods after publication and note when you made the edit. If impressions rise and clicks stay flat, look at the queries that account for the change. Some may be new and rank farther down. Others may show that readers expect a different format. That review gives you a specific next step instead of a reason to add the same phrase to every heading.

Turn the research into a useful writing brief

A practical brief starts with the intended reader and one clear question. For the flooring example, the reader is a homeowner trying to decide whether to repair an engineered floor. The main question is whether the floor can be refinished safely. Supporting questions can cover signs of a thin top layer, when a finish can be refreshed, and which details to provide when asking a contractor for a quote.

Choose the material the writer will need. A short decision table can show when to ask for an inspection, when a light refresh may help, and when to discuss replacement. Original photographs can show the difference between surface marks and damage through the wear layer. An example with clear limits gives people something they can apply while making their own decision.

Add internal links at the point where the reader would use them. Someone who has learned what to look for can follow a link to request an inspection or read how the service works. A related guide on materials can link to the refinishing page when the question comes up. Use link text that tells people what they will get, such as “how our floor inspection works.”

Before handing over the brief, write one sentence describing how you will evaluate the page. For an informational guide, you might monitor relevant queries, visits, and clicks to the service page. For a commercial landing page, qualified calls or form submissions may matter more. Use the measure that matches the job you picked at the beginning.

Questions to ask before paying for access

Look at the time you actually spend on research. A freelancer who investigates one client at a time needs a different setup from an agency researching many websites. Write down how many domains and locations you typically check, whether you need to export your lists, and whether colleagues need their own access. Compare those requirements against the current offer and Mangools' published plan details.

If you are looking for a KWFinder discount, check the billing term and the amount charged at checkout. Find out whether an advertised price covers an entire subscription or a limited access period. Confirm which features are available, how lookup limits work, and what happens to saved lists when access ends. Take a note of any answers you need from the seller before you commit.

Try a representative task when an evaluation option is available. Pick a real client question, review related keywords, inspect two competing pages, and build a brief with a few useful ideas. Time the task from start to finish. That gives you a clearer way to judge the value of access than the number of keywords returned by a single search.

Frequently asked questions

Is KWFinder useful for a new website? It can help you find specific topics and understand what kinds of pages already serve them. Start with a subject where you can offer something concrete, such as an example, an original photo, or a useful comparison. Build around the work you can do well.

What is a good keyword difficulty score? Compare scores within the same set of candidate terms and review the actual results. A useful keyword is one that fits your audience, matches a page you can build, and gives you a credible way to answer the searcher's question.

Should I create a page for every keyword? Group terms that share the same intent. Give readers one strong page that answers the related questions and create a separate page when the intent or the expected result changes.

Does search volume tell me how many visits I will get? The estimate describes searches. Visits depend on how often your page appears, where it appears, and whether people choose it. Use Search Console to measure what happened on your own site after the page has been live long enough to compare.

What should I check first after publishing? Verify that the page can be indexed and that its internal links work. Once there is enough data, look at which queries lead to the page and decide whether the next edit should clarify the title, improve the answer, or add a useful example.
